    "explanation": "The `max_tokens` answer cap is now enforced on `generated - reasoning_tokens`, and a token is classed as reasoning by a text heuristic: any thinking marker has been seen in the output so far (`answer != raw`) and the token did not lengthen the stripped answer. That heuristic is steered by model output, which in turn is steered by untrusted prompt content (the client sends tweet text to this endpoint for labelling). Two ways it misclassifies answer tokens as free reasoning: (1) once any think/channel block has appeared, `answer != raw` stays true for the rest of the reply, so every later answer token whose streamed text segment is empty (streaming detokenizers buffer partial words and UTF-8 sequences and emit \"\") is counted as reasoning; (2) injected text that makes the model emit `<think>`, `<|channel>` or `<channel|>` without a close tag makes every later token count as reasoning. In both cases the caller's `max_tokens` no longer bounds generation; the only effective bound is `max_tokens + THINKING_HEADROOM_TOKENS`, so a request with `max_tokens=1` can occupy the single MLX thread for 2049 tokens. Before this change the generator was capped at exactly `max_tokens`. Impact is limited to extra compute on a local server, and an injected unclosed tag also blanks the answer.",
    "fix": "Track thinking state explicitly (inside or outside an open block) instead of inferring it from answer length, and only exempt tokens emitted while a block is open. Cap `reasoning_tokens` at THINKING_HEADROOM_TOKENS separately from the answer budget, and treat zero-text tokens outside a block as answer tokens.",

    "confidence": 0.35,

    "filePath": "mlx-server/server.py",
    "category": "resource-exhaustion",
    "vulnerableCode": "raw += response.text\n...\nanswer = _remove_thinking(raw)",
    "explanation": "`_collect_reply` re-runs `_remove_thinking` over the entire accumulated output after every generated token. That function applies the lazy DOTALL regex `<think>.*?</think>` plus the Gemma channel scan, so the cost per reply is at least quadratic in output length. If the output contains many `<think>` openers with no closer (which prompt content can induce), each regex call is itself quadratic, making the whole reply roughly cubic. `ChatCompletionRequest.max_tokens` has no upper bound in `schemas.py`, and all of this runs on the single MLX worker thread, so one request with a large `max_tokens` and a prompt that elicits repeated `<think>` can stall chat and embedding requests for every client. Previously stripping ran once per reply. Low confidence on practical impact: the server is local and per-token model inference normally dominates until outputs get long.",

refuted.reason: A hard cap bounds the described overrun. Both generators pass `max_tokens + THINKING_HEADROOM_TOKENS` (fixed 2048) to the stream, so misclassified tokens can never push generation past that constant. The headroom is the documented design (server.py:466-470: thinking tokens are not counted and the caller's cap 'bounds the thinking'); a model that genuinely thinks spends the same budget, so prompt-injected tweet text gains nothing beyond what the design already grants. The worst case is about 2048 extra tokens on a server bound to 127.0.0.1 (server.py:638) with a single worker (server.py:82). The only caller-controlled lever, `max_tokens`, belongs to the local user, who is also the victim.
